title: Hari Singh Nalwa
hook: his great general held the north-west frontier and died at Jamrud
tomorrow: The Maharaja at the Akal Takht

segments.voice: Yesterday, a modern army: European drill under officers like Ventura, Sikh command, and a king willing to learn. Your line was learn from all. Who did you learn something from? Today, one of the generals who led that army. Day nine hundred fourteen.

Rocky hills. A narrow pass climbing west into the mountains: the Khyber. At its mouth stands a fort called Jamrud, and inside it a small garrison is waiting for a fight. Somewhere in the hills an army is coming down. The man responsible for this edge of the kingdom is a general whose name, the stories say, had become a word for nerve. When he falls, the fort still has to hold. Today: Hari Singh Nalwa.
screen: `THE MOUTH OF THE KHYBER.` → `A SMALL GARRISON AT JAMRUD.` → `A NAME THAT MEANT NERVE.`

segments.voice: First, the name. Tradition explains Nalwa with a story: on a hunt, a tiger sprang at the young Hari Singh, and he fought it and killed it. Whether every detail is true or not, the name stuck to him like armor. Next, the job. Ranjit Singh's kingdom reached toward the mountains of the north-west, toward Peshawar and the Khyber. That edge was hard to hold: rough country, local powers with their own claims, and a kingdom in Kabul that claimed the same ground. Hari Singh Nalwa was sent to hold it. He governed, built forts, and kept the passes. Then Jamrud. Tradition tells it like this. An Afghan army came down to the fort. Hari Singh rode out to relieve it and was mortally wounded in the fighting. And as he lay dying, he asked his men to keep his death a secret, so that the defenders and the enemy alike would think he was still in command, until help could arrive. They did. Tradition says the fort held. In the Guru Granth Sahib, the saint Kabir says the true hero is the one who fights for the deen, a word some read as the helpless and some as the faith, and who would be cut to pieces before leaving the field. Some Sikhs hear that line in stories like this one. Notice what the story honors. Not glory, not the size of the battle. A man who stood at the edge so others could live behind it, and who even in dying thought about who would hold the line. The frontier held.
screen: `NALWA: A NAME FROM A TIGER STORY.` · `SENT TO HOLD THE NORTH-WEST.` · `KEEP MY DEATH A SECRET.` · `THE HERO NEVER LEAVES THE FIELD.` · then, large: `THE FRONTIER HELD.`

segments.voice: Two minutes on your own frontier. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind the people who count on you right now: someone at home, a friend, a team, a patient, a class. Then think of your worst kind of day, tired, hurting, short on patience. On that day, what is the one thing you would still do for them? Name it plainly. Feel your feet on the floor while you hold it. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Nalwa, the name a tiger fight gave Hari Singh, Ranjit Singh's general on the north-west frontier, who died at Jamrud and, tradition says, kept the fort holding even then. Today's word.
Your line: the frontier held. Today, at your most tired moment, do the one thing someone is counting on you for anyway. Day nine hundred fourteen.

howItsDone: Sikhs tell stories of Hari Singh Nalwa as a general of great courage, and some connect his story with Kabir's verse about the true hero who never leaves the field.

fork.setup: you're the general, mortally wounded near Jamrud. the fort is under attack and help hasn't arrived. what do you ask of your men?
options: tell everyone at once that you're dying.
abandon the fort and save themselves.
keep your death a secret until help arrives.
fork.reveal: tradition says he asked them to hide his death, so the line would hold. they did, and the fort held.

original.note: Gurmukhi for Hari Singh Nalwa, Ranjit Singh's general on the north-west frontier.

what a scholar hears: the tiger story and the hidden death are tradition; some Sikhs hear in them Kabir's line about the hero who never leaves the field.

Claims rule: the year 1837 is removed from the hook field and never spoken.
The tiger story behind 'Nalwa' is tradition (some explain the name differently, e.g. a comparison to Raja Nal); framed as tradition. Confirm.
The request to keep his death secret until relief arrived: tradition; confirm wording. 'The fort held' attributed to tradition.
Afghan forces are named only as 'an Afghan army' and 'a powerful kingdom in Kabul'; 'proud tribes, rough country' is meant respectfully. Confirm the framing is fair.

Ang 1105, Kabir: 'soora so pahichaaneeai jo larai deen ke het; purjaa purjaa kat marai kabahoo na chhaadai khet'. Paraphrased as fighting 'for the sake of the helpless'; deen is read as 'the helpless/poor' by some and 'faith' by others. Confirm paraphrase.
